hints: Start from the measured gas volume, $462 \text{ cm}^3$. Recall the volume occupied by one mole of any gas under room conditions to convert volume into moles.
Once you have moles of $\text{H}_2$, think how to scale up from moles to individual molecules using the Avogadro constant.
walkthrough:
Turn gas volume into moles**
You have $462 \text{ cm}^3$ of hydrogen measured under room conditions. At room conditions one mole of gas occupies $24000 \text{ cm}^3$. So you are simply asking what fraction of a mole is $462 \text{ cm}^3$. $$\text{moles H}_2 = \frac{462}{24000} = 0.01925 \text{ mol}$$ Keep the extra figures for now to avoid rounding error.

Turn moles into molecules**
One mole contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ particles. Multiply your moles by this number: $$N = 0.01925 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 1.16 \times 10^{22}$$ So about $1.16 \times 10^{22}$ hydrogen molecules are produced. Give at least 2 significant figures.

Final answer: moles $\text{H}_2 = 462 / 24000 = 0.01925 \text{ mol}$
number of molecules $= 0.01925 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 1.16 \times 10^{22}$

hints: Write the cathode half-equation for formation of $\text{H}_2$ from $\text{H}^+$ and look at how many electrons are needed per $\text{H}_2$ molecule.
walkthrough:
Use the half-equation to find electrons per molecule**
At the cathode: $$2\text{H}^+ + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2(\text{g})$$ Each $\text{H}_2$ molecule needs $2$ electrons. So just double your answer from (a): $$N_{e} = 2 \times 1.16 \times 10^{22} = 2.32 \times 10^{22}$$

hints: Recall the charge carried by a single electron, $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, and think how total charge scales with total number of electrons.
walkthrough:
Multiply particle count by charge per electron**
Charge is additive. Each electron carries $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, so: $$Q = N_e \times e = 2.32 \times 10^{22} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$$ $$Q = 3.71 \times 10^{3} \text{ C}$$ This is the total charge passed through the cell.

hints: Link charge, current and time with $Q = It$ and remember to convert the electrolysis time of 14.0 minutes into seconds before substituting.
walkthrough:
Rearrange Q = It and fix the units**
Current in amps means coulombs per second, so time must be in seconds: $$t = 14.0 \times 60 = 840 \text{ s}$$ $$I = \frac{Q}{t}$$ $$x = \frac{3.71 \times 10^{3}}{840} = 4.42 \text{ A}$$ About $4.4 \text{ A}$ to 2 significant figures.

hints: Apply $\Delta S^{\ominus} = \Sigma S^{\ominus}(\text{products}) - \Sigma S^{\ominus}(\text{reactants})$, remembering to multiply each $S^{\ominus}$ value by its stoichiometric coefficient in $2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2$.
walkthrough:
Weight each entropy by its coefficient**
Think products minus reactants, not just one of each. For $$2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2(\text{g}) + \text{O}_2(\text{g})$$ $$\Delta S^{\ominus} = [2S^{\ominus}(\text{H}_2) + S^{\ominus}(\text{O}_2)] - [2S^{\ominus}(\text{H}_2\text{O})]$$ $$\Delta S^{\ominus} = [2(131) + 205] - [2(70)] = 467 - 140 = +327 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$$ The positive sign makes sense because you make 3 moles of disordered gas from liquid.

hints: Recall the Gibbs equation linking $\Delta G^{\ominus}$, $\Delta H^{\ominus}$, temperature and $\Delta S^{\ominus}$.

Check units before substituting: $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ is in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ but $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ is in $\text{J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$, so convert $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ to $\text{kJ K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$ by dividing by 1000.
walkthrough:
Set up the Gibbs equation**
Free energy tells you about feasibility: $$\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$$ You are given $\Delta H^{\ominus} = +572 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, $T = 298 \text{ K}$ and $\Delta S^{\ominus} = +327 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$ from (i).

Align kJ with J then calculate**
Convert entropy to kJ: $327/1000 = 0.327 \text{ kJ K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$. Then: $$\Delta G^{\ominus} = 572 - 298 \times 0.327$$ $$\Delta G^{\ominus} = 572 - 97.45 = +474.6 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The large positive value shows the splitting of water is highly non feasible under standard conditions at 298 K, which is why electrolysis needs electrical work.

Final answer: $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$
$\Delta G^{\ominus} = 572 - (298 \times 0.327) = +474.6 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Look at the sign of $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ from (i) and consider what happens to the $-T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ term in $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ as $T$ increases.
walkthrough:
See how temperature weights the entropy term**
Here $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ is positive (unfavourable) but $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ is also positive (favourable, more gas). In $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$, raising $T$ makes $T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ larger, so $-T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ becomes more negative. That pulls $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ down, so the reaction becomes more feasible, more spontaneous, at high temperature.

Final answer: Reaction becomes more feasible / more spontaneous at higher temperature as $T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ becomes more positive so $-T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ becomes more negative and $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ decreases.
